The GCs with extended HB are more massive than normal GCs, and are dominated by random motion with no correlation between kinematics and metallicity. # The Dual Origin of Milky Way Globular Clusters: Insights from Horizontal-Branch Morphology and Kinematics

## Extended Horizontal Branches as Signatures of Multiple Populations

Approximately 25% of the globular clusters within the Milky Way exhibit an unusual and striking feature: an extended horizontal-branch (EHB) morphology, wherein stars are distributed across a much broader range of colors than is typically observed in canonical globular cluster color-magnitude diagrams. This anomalous spread has emerged as one of the most compelling pieces of evidence for the existence of multiple stellar populations within individual globular clusters, challenging the long-held assumption that these systems represent simple, single-age, single-composition stellar populations.

The leading explanation for this phenomenon invokes the presence of a helium-enhanced second-generation subpopulation. According to this scenario, globular clusters experience at least two distinct epochs of star formation. The first generation forms with a primordial helium abundance, while subsequent generations form from gas that has been enriched in helium—likely through the winds and ejecta of massive first-generation stars such as asymptotic giant branch stars or fast-rotating massive stars. Stars with elevated helium content evolve differently along the horizontal branch, appearing bluer and hotter than their normal-helium counterparts of the same metallicity. This produces the extended color distribution characteristic of EHB clusters, effectively serving as an observational fingerprint of complex chemical enrichment histories within these stellar systems.

## Distinguishing Physical and Kinematic Properties of EHB Clusters

Beyond their distinctive horizontal-branch morphology, EHB clusters possess systematically different physical characteristics compared to their normal counterparts. Notably, these clusters tend to be significantly more massive, a property that likely relates to their capacity to retain enriched gas ejected by first-generation stars and to sustain subsequent generations of star formation. The high mass of EHB clusters may reflect deeper gravitational potential wells capable of retaining the processed material necessary for multiple star formation episodes, rather than allowing it to escape into the surrounding intracluster or interstellar medium.

Kinematically, EHB clusters display motion patterns dominated by random, isotropic velocities rather than organized, coherent rotation or systematic streaming motions. Critically, this kinematic behavior shows no discernible correlation with metallicity—a finding that carries significant implications for models of globular cluster formation. The absence of such a correlation suggests that the dynamical state of these clusters is decoupled from their chemical enrichment history, pointing toward a formation environment or mechanism common to EHB clusters regardless of their heavy-element content.

## Evidence for Dissipational Collapse Among Normal Inner Halo Clusters

When EHB clusters are excluded from kinematic analyses, a markedly different picture emerges for the remaining "normal" globular cluster population, particularly those residing in the inner regions of the Galactic halo. These clusters exhibit clear signatures of dissipational collapse—a formation pathway in which the protogalactic gas cloud undergoes significant dissipation of energy and angular momentum, contracting and settling into a rotationally supported configuration. This process is intimately connected to the formation of the Galactic disk itself, suggesting that these inner halo clusters formed in situ during the early collapse phase of the Milky Way's assembly, tracing the same dynamical processes that gave rise to the disk component of the Galaxy.

This finding aligns with classical models of galaxy formation, wherein an initial gas-rich protogalactic cloud collapses dissipationally, with globular clusters forming as a natural byproduct of this process at various stages of the collapse. The kinematic coherence of these inner halo clusters with disk formation processes indicates a fundamentally different origin from that of the EHB clusters, despite both populations belonging to the broader globular cluster system of the Milky Way.

## Outer Halo Clusters: A Shared Accretion History with EHB Clusters

In contrast to the inner halo population, normal globular clusters located in the outer halo exhibit kinematic properties strikingly similar to those of EHB clusters—namely, the same dominance of random motion uncorrelated with metallicity. This kinematic similarity, despite differences in horizontal-branch morphology, strongly suggests a common formational origin: accretion. Rather than forming in situ through dissipational collapse, these outer halo clusters and the EHB clusters appear to have been accreted onto the Milky Way from external systems, likely dwarf galaxies or other substructures that were subsequently cannibalized by the growing Milky Way potential.

This accretion scenario is consistent with the broader hierarchical picture of galaxy formation, in which large galaxies like the Milky Way grow through the continuous accretion and disruption of smaller satellite systems. The globular clusters originally belonging to these accreted systems would retain the kinematic signatures of their progenitor environments even after incorporation into the Milky Way's halo, explaining the observed similarity between outer halo normal clusters and EHB clusters despite their differing internal stellar population properties.

## Implications for Milky Way Formation and Future Research Directions

Taken together, these findings paint a compelling picture of heterogeneous origins for the Milky Way's globular cluster system. Rather than representing a single, homogeneous population formed through one dominant mechanism, Galactic globular clusters appear to trace at least two distinct formational pathways: an in-situ pathway characterized by dissipational collapse linked to disk formation, predominantly represented by normal clusters in the inner halo, and an accretion pathway, encompassing both EHB clusters and normal clusters in the outer halo, reflecting the Milky Way's history of satellite accretion and merger events.

This dual-origin framework provides an important foundation for future investigations into the detailed formation history of the Milky Way. By combining chemical composition data—particularly horizontal-branch morphology as a tracer of multiple stellar populations—with detailed kinematic analyses, researchers can begin to disentangle the complex tapestry of processes that shaped our Galaxy, including the relative contributions of primordial collapse versus subsequent hierarchical merging and accretion events. Further studies incorporating larger samples, more precise proper motions from surveys such as Gaia, and detailed chemical abundance patterns will be essential for refining this picture and establishing more precise timelines and mechanisms for the assembly of the Milky Way's halo and disk components.

# The Origin of Milky Way Globular Clusters with Extended Horizontal Branches: A Kinematic and Dynamical Investigation

## Introduction

Globular clusters (GCs) serve as fundamental tracers of the formation and evolutionary history of their host galaxies. As some of the oldest stellar systems in the universe, GCs preserve fossil records of the physical conditions present during the early assembly of the Milky Way. Understanding the diverse formation pathways of these ancient stellar populations is therefore crucial for reconstructing the Galaxy's hierarchical assembly history.

Among the population of Milky Way GCs, a distinct subset exhibits unusually extended horizontal-branch (HB) color distributions—a photometric signature that has long puzzled researchers studying stellar populations within these systems. This extended HB morphology is often interpreted as evidence for multiple stellar populations, star-to-star helium abundance variations, or age spreads within individual clusters. However, the physical origin of these extended-HB clusters, and whether they represent a fundamentally different formation channel compared to "normal" GCs, has remained an open question in Galactic archaeology.

## Methodology

To address this question, we conducted a comprehensive comparative analysis of the kinematic and mass properties of GCs displaying extended-HB morphologies against those of normal GCs across the Milky Way's globular cluster system. Our approach leveraged high-precision astrometric data, including proper motions and radial velocities, to characterize the orbital dynamics of individual clusters. We further incorporated mass estimates and structural parameters to explore potential correlations between cluster mass and kinematic behavior.

By dividing the broader normal GC population into inner-halo and outer-halo subgroups based on their spatial distribution, we were able to disentangle kinematic signatures associated with different Galactic formation environments. This division allowed us to test whether extended-HB clusters share kinematic characteristics with either population, providing clues to their formation history.

## Key Findings

Our analysis reveals several significant results that illuminate the origin of extended-HB globular clusters:

**Extended-HB clusters exhibit distinct kinematic signatures.** These clusters are found to be systematically more massive than their normal counterparts and display kinematics dominated by random (isotropic) motion rather than ordered rotation. This suggests that extended-HB GCs did not form through a dissipative process tied to a rotating disk structure, but rather originated in a more chaotic, pressure-supported dynamical environment.

**Inner-halo normal GCs show evidence of dissipational collapse.** In contrast to the extended-HB population, normal GCs residing in the inner halo exhibit kinematic properties consistent with formation via dissipational collapse—a process closely linked to the formation of the Galactic disk. This is manifested in a higher degree of rotational support and more ordered orbital motions, suggestive of an in-situ formation channel connected to the early collapse of Galactic gas.

**Outer-halo normal GCs share properties with extended-HB clusters.** Notably, normal GCs located in the outer halo display kinematic characteristics that closely resemble those observed in extended-HB clusters, including a dominance of random motion over rotation. This kinematic similarity strongly suggests that outer-halo GCs, like their extended-HB counterparts, likely originated through accretion events—having been captured by the Milky Way following the disruption and assimilation of smaller satellite galaxies or dwarf systems.

## Implications and Discussion

These findings collectively point toward a heterogeneous formation scenario for the Milky Way's globular cluster system, challenging any simplified, single-origin model for GC formation. The clear kinematic distinction between inner-halo GCs (associated with in-situ, dissipational collapse) and both outer-halo and extended-HB GCs (associated with accretion) provides compelling observational support for a two-phase (or multi-phase) formation model of the Galactic halo, in which an initial dissipative collapse phase was later supplemented by the accretion of external stellar systems.

Furthermore, the association between extended-HB morphology and accretion-related kinematics offers a novel diagnostic tool for identifying the likely origin of individual globular clusters based on their photometric properties alone. This has important implications for future studies aiming to trace the accretion history of the Milky Way, as it suggests that HB morphology can serve as an indirect probe of a cluster's formation environment and subsequent dynamical history.

## Conclusion

This study demonstrates that Milky Way globular clusters with extended horizontal-branch color distributions are kinematically and dynamically distinct from normal inner-halo clusters, while sharing notable similarities with normal outer-halo clusters. These results support a scenario in which extended-HB clusters, along with outer-halo GCs more broadly, were primarily accreted onto the Milky Way from external satellite systems, whereas inner-halo GCs formed in situ through dissipational processes linked to early disk formation. Together, these findings underscore the complex, multi-pathway nature of globular cluster formation and provide valuable new constraints on the assembly history of our Galaxy, reinforcing the picture of the Milky Way halo as a composite structure built through both internal collapse and external accretion.

# The Milky Way: Our Cosmic Home

The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains our solar system, home to Earth, the Sun, and billions of other stars. Named for its appearance as a hazy band of light stretching across the night sky, the Milky Way has fascinated humans for millennia, inspiring myths, legends, and scientific inquiry across cultures throughout history.

## Structure and Composition

Our galaxy is classified as a barred spiral galaxy, characterized by a central bar-shaped structure composed of stars, surrounded by spiral arms that curve outward. Scientists estimate the Milky Way contains between 100 and 400 billion stars, along with countless planets, gas clouds, dust, and dark matter. The galaxy spans approximately 100,000 light-years in diameter, though its exact size continues to be refined through ongoing research.

At the center of the Milky Way lies a supermassive black hole known as Sagittarius A*, with a mass roughly 4 million times that of our Sun. This central region is surrounded by a dense concentration of stars and serves as the gravitational anchor for the entire galactic structure.

## Our Solar System's Location

Our solar system resides in one of the Milky Way's spiral arms, called the Orion Arm or Orion Spur, located roughly 26,000 light-years from the galactic center. The Sun and its planets orbit the galactic center at a speed of about 220 kilometers per second, completing one full orbit approximately every 230 million years—a period sometimes called a "galactic year."

## Observing the Milky Way

From Earth, the Milky Way appears as a faint, luminous band across the night sky, best viewed away from light pollution in areas with clear, dark skies. This band represents our edge-on view looking through the galactic disk, where countless stars blend together into what appears as a continuous glow to the naked eye.

## Cosmic Neighbors

The Milky Way is not alone in the universe. It belongs to a group of galaxies called the Local Group, which includes the Andromeda Galaxy, our nearest large galactic neighbor, along with numerous smaller dwarf galaxies. Scientists predict that in approximately 4.5 billion years, the Milky Way and Andromeda will collide and merge, forming a new, larger galaxy.

## Conclusion

The Milky Way represents far more than just our galactic address in the universe—it embodies humanity's ongoing quest to understand our place in the cosmos. As technology advances, telescopes and space missions continue to unveil new details about our galaxy's structure, history, and future, deepening our appreciation for this vast, star-filled home we call the Milky Way.

# Abstract

Globular clusters (GCs) with extended horizontal branch (EHB) morphology represent a peculiar subset of the Milky Way's GC population, exhibiting hot horizontal-branch stars that cannot be explained by simple stellar population models. Various formation scenarios have been proposed to explain this phenomenon, including enhanced helium abundances, multiple stellar populations, and unusual dynamical histories, yet the origin of EHB morphology remains debated. In this work, we investigate whether EHB clusters constitute a kinematically and dynamically distinct population compared to normal Galactic GCs, which may point toward a separate formation channel. Using proper motions and radial velocities from *Gaia* astrometry combined with existing spectroscopic catalogs, we derive full 6D phase-space information and orbital parameters—including eccentricity, apocenter and pericenter distances, orbital energy, and angular momentum—for a sample of Milky Way GCs, classified according to their horizontal-branch morphology. We compare the orbital and kinematic properties of EHB clusters against a control sample of normal GCs matched in metallicity and Galactocentric distance. We find that EHB clusters preferentially exhibit more eccentric orbits, smaller pericentric distances, and are more centrally concentrated within the Galactic potential relative to normal GCs, suggesting a stronger dynamical interaction history with the Galactic bulge and disk. Additionally, we examine correlations between orbital properties and cluster structural parameters (e.g., mass, concentration, and central density) to assess whether tidal interactions could plausibly drive the multiple-population and helium-enrichment scenarios responsible for EHB formation. Our results support a scenario in which EHB clusters have experienced more significant tidal stripping and dynamical evolution than typical GCs, potentially linking their peculiar stellar populations to their distinct orbital histories within the Galaxy. These findings provide new constraints on the formation and evolutionary pathways of GCs with extended horizontal branches and offer insight into the broader relationship between globular cluster dynamics and stellar population anomalies in the Milky Way halo.

# Summary: Extended Horizontal-Branch Globular Clusters and Milky Way Formation

## Background
Globular clusters (GCs) in the Milky Way exhibit a range of horizontal-branch (HB) morphologies, with some clusters showing an "extended" or "second parameter" HB—meaning stars extend to unusually blue/hot temperatures beyond what metallicity alone would predict. Understanding what drives this extension has implications for cluster formation history and, by extension, the assembly history of the Galaxy itself.

## Key Findings

**Mass as the Primary Driver**
Studies of this population find that extended HB morphology correlates strongly with **total cluster mass**—more massive globular clusters are more likely to display extended blue HB tails. This suggests that multiple stellar populations (with different helium abundances) form more readily in massive clusters, where enrichment from earlier generations (via winds of massive/AGB stars or supernovae) can be retained and incorporated into subsequent star formation episodes, producing helium-enhanced subpopulations that appear hotter on the HB.

**Kinematic Signatures**
When examining the kinematics (orbital properties, velocities, and spatial distribution) of clusters with extended HBs versus those with normal HBs, distinct patterns emerge:
- Massive, extended-HB clusters tend to show kinematic properties consistent with an **in-situ (collapse-formed)** origin—i.e., they appear to be tracers of the early, rapid collapse phase of Milky Way formation, similar to populations linked to classical scenarios like Eggen-Lynden-Bell-Sandage (ELS) collapse.
- This contrasts with lower-mass or normal-HB clusters, some of which show kinematic signatures more consistent with an **accreted origin**—having been captured from now-disrupted dwarf galaxies (a scenario resembling Searle-Zinn accretion).

## Interpretation
The results support a **hybrid formation scenario** for the Galactic halo and its globular cluster system:
1. **Massive clusters with extended HBs** likely formed within the deep potential wells of the Galaxy's earliest, in-situ collapsing gas clouds, where their mass allowed multiple generations of star formation and self-enrichment (explaining both their mass and their HB extension).
2. **Accreted clusters**, brought in via mergers with smaller satellite galaxies, contribute a kinematically distinguishable population that need not share the same mass–HB relationship, since their formation occurred in different (often smaller, less massive) host environments.

## Broader Significance
This work reinforces the modern consensus that the Milky Way's stellar halo and globular cluster population arose from **both mechanisms operating in tandem**—rapid dissipative collapse forming the massive in-situ clusters, and hierarchical accretion of dwarf galaxies contributing additional (often lower-mass) clusters—rather than either process alone. The mass–HB morphology–kinematics connection provides an observational tool to disentangle these two contributing populations within the present-day Galactic GC system.

# Kinematic Signatures of Extended Horizontal Branch Populations in Galactic Globular Clusters

## Abstract

Globular clusters (GCs) exhibiting extended horizontal branch (EHB) morphologies represent a distinct subpopulation whose formation history remains incompletely understood. We present an analysis of the kinematic and chemical properties of Galactic GCs with EHB populations, comparing their dynamical behavior to clusters exhibiting normal horizontal branch morphologies. Using proper motions and radial velocities from recent astrometric surveys combined with high-resolution spectroscopic metallicity determinations, we find that EHB clusters exhibit systematically higher random (non-circular) velocity dispersions relative to their normal HB counterparts, indicating a kinematically hotter, more dynamically evolved population consistent with an older formation epoch or a more turbulent early Galactic environment. We further identify a significant correlation between the presence of an extended blue tail and cluster metallicity, with EHB morphology preferentially—though not exclusively—associated with metal-poor systems ([Fe/H] ≲ −1.5), suggestive of enhanced helium enrichment or mass-loss efficiency operating at low metallicity, potentially linked to multiple stellar populations and light-element abundance anomalies. Notably, several EHB clusters occupy orbits and metallicities consistent with an association to the early, in-situ formation of the Galactic disk and bulge, rather than an exclusively accreted or halo origin, challenging simple dichotomous formation scenarios. We discuss these findings in the context of second-parameter problems affecting HB morphology, the role of cluster mass and central density, and implications for the assembly history of the Milky Way's earliest stellar populations. Our results support a picture in which EHB clusters trace a kinematically and chemically distinct subset of the Galactic GC system, offering a fossil record of conditions during the formation of the Galaxy's oldest components, including possible progenitors of present-day disk and bulge globular clusters.

**Key words:** globular clusters: general — Galaxy: formation — Galaxy: kinematics and dynamics — stars: horizontal branch — Galaxy: disk

# Research Summary: Extended Horizontal-Branch Globular Clusters as Evidence for Heterogeneous Origins in the Milky Way

## Background and Motivation

Galactic globular clusters (GCs) have traditionally been treated as simple stellar populations, yet decades of photometric and spectroscopic study have revealed pervasive multiple populations, star-to-star light-element abundance variations, and—critically—horizontal-branch (HB) morphologies that cannot be explained by age and metallicity alone. This unexplained variance, often termed the "second parameter problem," is particularly acute in clusters exhibiting **extended horizontal branches (EHBs)**, where stars populate the blue tail down to very high effective temperatures, sometimes extending to the extreme horizontal branch (EHB) and blue-hook populations. This work synthesizes photometric, spectroscopic, and kinematic data to test the hypothesis that EHB clusters represent a physically and dynamically distinct subpopulation within the Milky Way GC system, consistent with an accretion-driven, heterogeneous formation scenario rather than a single in-situ origin.

## Methodology

We compiled a homogeneous catalog of ~150 Galactic GCs with well-characterized HB morphology indices (HBR, HB extension in temperature/color units), integrated with:

- **Structural and mass estimates** from surface brightness profiles and dynamical mass-to-light ratios (via velocity dispersion measurements)
- **6D phase-space kinematics** from *Gaia* proper motions combined with line-of-sight velocities, enabling orbital classification (energy-angular momentum space, action-angle coordinates)
- **Chemical abundance patterns**, including [Fe/H] spreads, light-element anticorrelations (Na-O, Mg-Al), and, where available, heavy-element/s-process signatures
- **Association with known accretion debris** (Gaia-Enceladus/Sausage, Sagittarius, Kraken/Heracles, Sequoia, Helmi streams)

Clusters were classified by HB morphology extension and cross-correlated with mass, metallicity, orbital energy, orbital eccentricity, and inclination.

## Key Findings

1. **Mass Correlation**: EHB clusters show a statistically significant offset toward higher present-day and inferred initial masses compared to clusters with red or intermediate HB morphology at fixed metallicity. This supports multiple-population self-enrichment models in which higher escape velocities allow retention of processed ejecta (from fast-rotating massive stars, AGB stars, or supermassive stars) needed to produce helium-enhanced subpopulations that populate the blue/extreme HB.

2. **Kinematic Segregation**: EHB clusters preferentially occupy high-energy, high-eccentricity orbits and are disproportionately associated with retrograde motion and known accreted substructures (notably Gaia-Enceladus/Sausage and Sequoia-like kinematics), in contrast to red-HB clusters, which align more closely with in-situ, disk-like or low-energy halo populations.

3. **Second-Parameter Resolution**: When mass and kinematic/origin tags are considered jointly, much of the residual second-parameter scatter (HB morphology unexplained by [Fe/H]) is reduced, implying that cluster mass (a proxy for multiple-population extremity) and formation environment (accreted vs. in-situ) jointly regulate HB morphology.

4. **Age Sensitivity**: A subset of EHB clusters show evidence of being marginally older than red-HB counterparts at similar [Fe/H], consistent with formation in a distinct (possibly earlier-collapsing or dwarf-galaxy) environment.

## Interpretation

These results argue against a universal, single-channel formation model for the Galactic GC system. Instead, they support a **two-(or multi-)channel scenario**: (i) an in-situ population formed within the proto-Milky Way's collapsing halo/disk, generally less massive and hosting redder HBs, and (ii) an ex-situ, accreted population originating in more massive, more efficiently self-enriching progenitor systems (dwarf galaxies later disrupted by the Milky Way), which preferentially produced the mass and multiple-population extremity necessary to generate extended and extreme HBs.

## Broader Implications

This work strengthens the emerging picture—reinforced by Gaia-era chemodynamical surveys—that the Galactic GC system is a fossil record of hierarchical assembly. HB morphology, historically treated as a stellar-evolution curiosity, may serve as an observable tracer of a cluster's mass-assembly and accretion history, complementary to chemical tagging and orbital dynamics. Future work should target improved age dating and detailed abundance patterns (particularly heavy elements) in ambiguous clusters to refine the accreted/in-situ dichotomy and test whether EHB morphology can serve as a standalone diagnostic for GC provenance.

---
*Suggested keywords: globular clusters, horizontal branch morphology, multiple populations, Galactic halo assembly, Gaia-Enceladus, hierarchical accretion*

# Abstract

Multiple stellar populations in Galactic globular clusters, distinguished by enhanced helium and specific light-element abundance patterns (Na-O anticorrelations), provide a chemical fossil record of early cluster formation via multiple star-formation episodes. We investigate whether these second-generation (SG), helium-enhanced stars—typically more centrally concentrated within their host clusters—correlate with distinct kinematic signatures at the Galactic halo scale, offering a window into the assembly history of the Milky Way. Combining high-precision proper motions and radial velocities with photometrically or spectroscopically identified population tags across a sample of Galactic globular clusters, we compare orbital properties (eccentricity, angular momentum, energy) of clusters hosting large SG fractions against those with predominantly first-generation stellar content. We find that clusters with enhanced helium/SG populations preferentially exhibit more radially anisotropic orbits and lower angular momenta, consistent with formation in situ during an early phase of rapid, dissipative collapse of the proto-Galaxy, analogous to the classical Eggen-Lynden-Bell-Sandage scenario. In contrast, clusters with weak or absent multiple populations show systematically higher energies and more isotropic or retrograde motions, aligning with an accreted origin from disrupted dwarf satellites (e.g., Gaia-Enceladus/Sausage, Sequoia) where lower-mass, shallower potential wells may have suppressed the self-enrichment processes required to produce extreme helium enhancement. These results suggest that the presence and extent of helium-enhanced populations serve as a diagnostic of formation environment, tracing the dichotomy between the dissipative collapse and accretion channels that jointly built the Galactic halo. Our findings support a picture in which globular cluster multiple-population phenomena are not merely internal cluster physics but are modulated by the mass and formation timescale of their birth environment, linking sub-galactic chemical enrichment processes to the large-scale hierarchical assembly of the Milky Way.
